title: The 7-Question Storm Knock
summary: Disarm in 15 seconds, diagnose in 4 questions, decide on the ladder — the door script that books one inspection per eight doors in active storm territory.
body_markdown:
## The frame in three phases

The 7-Question Storm Knock has been A/B-tested against roughly 30 variations across hundreds of reps over a decade. Nothing has beaten it for post-storm canvassing inside the 14-day window. It works because it's organized around what the homeowner is feeling, not what the rep wants to say.

Three phases: **Disarm, Diagnose, Decide.**

Learn the phases, then the questions inside them.

## Phase 1 — Disarm (first 15 seconds)

The homeowner had their hand on the door, ready to close it. You have about 15 seconds to give them a reason to leave it open.

The opener:

> "Hey, I'm [Name] with Roof Pitcher. I'm not here to sell you anything — I'm doing free 60-second damage checks on this street after the storm Tuesday."

Three words do almost all the work in that sentence:

**"Not here to sell."** Say it within the first 5 words. The homeowner has been pitched by three guys today. The pattern interrupt buys you another 10 seconds.

**"Free 60-second."** People will give a stranger 60 seconds. They will not give a stranger 5 minutes. Anchor on a tiny commitment.

**"This street."** Implies you're not random. You're working the block methodically. That makes you a professional, not a hustler.

Delivery rules:

- Eye contact. Not aggressive — friendly.
- Half-step back, not forward. Give them space.
- Clipboard visible. Tablet in your other hand.
- No business card yet. Cards trigger "this is a sales call." Cards come at the end if at all.

## Phase 2 — Diagnose (the 7 questions, in order)

You don't ask all 7 every time. You ask until you get a clear signal. Most successful door knocks stop at question 4. The questions are tools — pick the next one based on what they said.

**Question 1: "Have you had anyone up there yet?"**

- If **yes** → go to Q2 (find out if you're really competing).
- If **no** → skip to Q4 (go straight to booking the inspection).

**Question 2: "Did they leave you a written scope?"**

If yes, they may be locked in with another contractor. Ask if they're happy with the scope. If they're not, the door is open.

**Question 3: "Have you filed with insurance yet?"**

This is the single most important question in storm sales. The whole conversation pivots on the answer.

- If **no** → you have a wide-open opportunity. Move to Q4 immediately.
- If **yes** → ask if the claim is approved or pending. If pending, ask if they need help with the adjuster meeting (you'll often get invited).

**Question 4: "Mind if I take a ladder up there real quick? 60 seconds, I'll show you photos either way."**

This is the close at the door. You are not asking for a sale. You are asking for an inspection. The phrase **"photos either way"** is critical — it tells them they win regardless of what you find. Most homeowners say yes to this if Q1-3 went well.

**Question 5: "Have you noticed any leaks or stains on ceilings recently?"**

Only use if Q4 gets a no. Surfaces hidden damage that wasn't visible from the curb. Re-opens the conversation about why an inspection might be worth doing today.

**Question 6: "How old is your roof, do you know?"**

Used to set context. Any roof 10+ years old just got a free new roof from the storm — the insurance approval threshold is very forgiving for older roofs with any storm damage. Mentioning the age out loud sometimes flips a no into a yes.

**Question 7: "If I find damage, would you want help walking through what filing a claim looks like?"**

The consent question. You're asking permission to help them later, not to sell now. Almost always works because they have nothing to lose. This is also the question that gets the spouse on the phone — "let me check with my wife real quick."

## Phase 3 — Decide (the 60 seconds on the ladder)

Question 4 got a yes. You're going up. This is where the inspection becomes the proof.

**Take 4–6 photos:**

1. **Wide shot of the worst slope** — gives context.
2. **Closeups of 3–4 hail hits** — use a chalk circle around each one so they show up clearly in the photo.
3. **Soft metals** — gutters, AC fins, vents. Hail almost always dents soft metals first. AC fins are the single most undeniable evidence on a property.
4. **Roof vent or pipe boot** — commonly missed by adjusters. Worth a supplement later.

**Come down.** Don't lecture from the top of the ladder. Don't lecture from the front door. Lean on the porch railing. Sit on the step. Body language matters more than wording.

**Show the photos calmly.** Zoom in on one hail hit. "See the circle? That's a hail impact. Here's another one. Here's the AC fin bent — that doesn't bend from wind, only ice impact."

**Offer two options.** Two, not three.

> "Here's what I found. Two options: file a claim and let's see what insurance says — costs you nothing — or do nothing and we'll come back in 6 months and check again. Which feels right?"

No urgency. No fear. Two clean choices. About 60–70% of inspected homeowners pick option 1 if the photos are real.

## What the script doesn't do

This script does not include closing language. It doesn't include pricing. It doesn't include warranty pitches. That's deliberate.

If the homeowner picks option 1 (file the claim), you move to Lesson 6 — the kitchen-table close. Don't try to close the contract at the door. Close the next step.

If the homeowner picks option 2 (do nothing), you leave gracefully. "Got it. I'll text you my number — call if anything changes. Thanks for letting me up there." Then walk away.

About 15% of "option 2" homeowners call you back within 30 days. That's free revenue you don't fight for. The reps who push at the door lose those callbacks because the homeowner remembers them as the pushy one.

## Practice the script before you knock

You will mangle this the first 20 times you say it. That's normal. Practice with another rep. Record yourself on your phone. Refine the rhythm.

The goal isn't memorization. The goal is the script becoming so natural it doesn't sound like a script. When it sounds natural, your close rate climbs. Until then, it sounds like you're reading off a card and homeowners feel it.

The difference between a 5% knock-to-book rep and a 15% knock-to-book rep is rarely talent. It's reps. Hundreds of doors. Practice the script.
key_takeaways: Three phases: Disarm (15 sec), Diagnose (≤7 questions), Decide (ladder).
Open with 'not here to sell you anything' in the first 5 words.
Question 4 is the close at the door — ask for the inspection, not the sale.
Show 4–6 photos with chalk circles. Soft metals = undeniable proof.
Two options at the end. Never three. Never urgency.

quiz.q: Why is 'I'm not here to sell you anything' so important in the opener?
choices: It interrupts the homeowner's sales-defense pattern
It signals you'll work for free
It makes the rep sound humble
quiz.explanation: The homeowner has been pitched 3 times today. The pattern interrupt buys you the next 10 seconds.

quiz.q: Question 4 — the ladder ask — is structured to do what?
choices: Close the contract at the door
Book the inspection without asking for a sale
quiz.explanation: Q4 closes the inspection, not the roof. The roof close happens at the kitchen table after the inspection.

quiz.q: How many photos should you take on the 60-second ladder check?
choices: 4–6 photos including soft metals and one wide shot
quiz.explanation: 4–6 photos: wide shot, 3-4 chalk-circled hits, soft metals, and a missed-supplement item like a pipe boot.

quiz.q: After showing photos, you offer how many options?
choices: Two — file the claim or do nothing
Three — file, finance, or pay cash
Four — file, finance, partial, or wait
quiz.explanation: Two clean options. Three+ options cause decision fatigue and trigger 'let me think about it.'

homework: Memorize the opener and Q1-Q4 by heart tonight. Tomorrow knock 30 doors and force yourself to use only those four. Track your booked-inspection rate. Most reps double their booking rate in week one just from script discipline.
